title: Autochthonous cases of mycetoma in Europe: report of two cases and review of literature
case_text:
Patient 2, a 46 year-old Albanian woodcutter, was a colleague and friend of patient 1 but had not dared to travel to Italy with him. He had started presenting signs of mycetoma on the right foot in 1982. After receiving several courses of antibiotics (penicillin plus gentamycin followed by other unspecified drugs) without response, he underwent a below-knee amputation in 1995. Nevertheless, the disease showed further progression, so an above-knee amputation was proposed, but he refused. He presented to the CTD in 2001, the year of his arrival in Italy. He presented a swollen stump with nodules and sinuses draining white granules. The specimens obtained through needle aspiration permitted to diagnose, again, a mycetoma due to Actinomadura madurae. The patient was successfully treated with antibiotic therapy, similarly to patient 1, and showed no recurrence during the 2 year-follow up (last visit in November, 2003, then he came back to Albania).
The cases in Albanian patients (including the two cases described in this paper) were diagnosed and reported in Greece and in Italy. All 5 patients had an infection caused by Actinomadura madurae. Of these 5 patients, 4 were treated exclusively with antibiotic therapy, only our patient 2 also had surgery. De Palma et al. describe an improvement 6 months after treatment. As for the cases described in Greece, one patient was lost to follow up about 5 weeks after the beginning of the treatment, while there are no details about the follow up of the other patient.
All Bulgarian cases are reported in a case series by Balabanoff published in 1980. A variety of causative agents is described, both fungal and bacterial. One patient with Madurella mycetomatis infection had the infected foot amputated. There is no information about the post-treatment follow up of the patients.
There were 3 patients of Greek origin. One patient was injured during a motorcycle accident in Crete, and developed an infection due to Nocardia asteroides (although also Sporothrix schenckii was isolated from the material obtained from the wound). Another Greek patient had a mycetoma on the forehead caused by Nocardia brasiliensis  and the third one developed a mycetoma of the foot caused by Actinomadura madurae . All these patients received specific medical treatment and no surgery was required. The authors report improvement of the infections from 7 to 9 months after treatment (no longer follow up is available).
Two case reports describe mycetoma of the foot caused by Actinomadura madurae in Italian women. Both patients had relapses/progression of the disease despite antibiotic therapy based on the antibiograms. After a further antibiotic course, one patient resulted stationary and the other one improved (but both cases were described shortly after the last therapeutic course). The third case was caused by Fusarium moniliforme and affected the foot of a retired miner.
Cases in Turkish patients were reported from Turkey and from the UK. In the first one, no causative agent was isolated from the material draining from the foot, while in the second one a mycetoma of the hand sustained by Streptomyces somaliensis was described. The latter case was treated with surgical intervention plus medical therapy for 10 months, obtaining resolution after one year.

distillation_prompt.system_prompt:
You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Mycetoma
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: Actinomycetoma caused by Actinomadura madurae
